topics.title: Topic Particle 은/는
topics.summary: The topic particle 은/는 marks what a sentence is about — use 은 after a consonant and 는 after a vowel.
topics.explanation: 은/는 marks the topic, the thing the sentence is commenting on, often with a sense of contrast. Attach 은 to a noun ending in a consonant and 는 to a noun ending in a vowel. It differs from the subject particle 이/가, which simply marks the grammatical subject.

examples.translation: I am a student.
The book is on the desk.
Today the weather is nice.

exercises.promptTranslation: I am Korean.
exercises.explanation: 저 ends in a vowel, so the topic particle 는 is used.

exercises.promptTranslation: My younger sibling is tall.
exercises.explanation: 동생 ends in a consonant, so 은 is used.

exercises.promptTranslation: The coffee is delicious.
exercises.explanation: 커피 ends in a vowel, so 는 is used.

exercises.promptTranslation: The mountain is high.
exercises.explanation: 산 ends in a consonant, so 은 is used.

topics.title: Subject Particle 이/가
topics.summary: The subject particle 이/가 marks the grammatical subject — use 이 after a consonant and 가 after a vowel.
topics.explanation: 이/가 marks the subject that performs the action or is described. Attach 이 to a noun ending in a consonant and 가 to a noun ending in a vowel. Compared with 은/는, 이/가 often introduces new or specific information.

examples.translation: A friend came.
The book is on the desk.
The weather is nice.

exercises.promptTranslation: A student is in the library.
exercises.explanation: 학생 ends in a consonant, so 이 is used.

exercises.promptTranslation: The wind is blowing.
exercises.explanation: 바람 ends in a consonant, so 이 is used.

exercises.promptTranslation: The child is sleeping.
exercises.explanation: 아이 ends in a vowel, so 가 is used.

exercises.promptTranslation: There is no time.
exercises.explanation: 시간 ends in a consonant, so 이 is used.

topics.title: Object Particle 을/를
topics.summary: The object particle 을/를 marks the direct object — use 을 after a consonant and 를 after a vowel.
topics.explanation: 을/를 marks the direct object, the thing the action is done to. Attach 을 to a noun ending in a consonant and 를 to a noun ending in a vowel.

examples.translation: I eat an apple.
I read a book.
I drink water.

exercises.promptTranslation: I watch a movie.
exercises.explanation: 영화 ends in a vowel, so 를 is used.

exercises.promptTranslation: I eat (a meal).
exercises.explanation: 밥 ends in a consonant, so 을 is used.

exercises.promptTranslation: I drink coffee.
exercises.explanation: 커피 ends in a vowel, so 를 is used.

exercises.promptTranslation: I make food.
exercises.explanation: 음식 ends in a consonant, so 을 is used.

topics.title: The Copula 이다 (to be)
topics.summary: Use 이에요/예요 to say "A is B" in polite Korean.
topics.explanation: Place the copula after the noun that describes something. If the noun ends with a consonant, use 이에요; if it ends with a vowel, use 예요. This form is polite and works in everyday sentences. The ending stays attached directly to the noun.

examples.translation: I am a student.
This book is interesting.
Seoul is the capital of Korea.

exercises.promptTranslation: That person is a teacher ___
exercises.explanation: 선생 ends with a consonant, so the polite copula is 이에요.

exercises.promptTranslation: This book is interesting ___
exercises.explanation: 재미 ends with a vowel, so the polite copula is 예요.

exercises.promptTranslation: I am a student ___
exercises.explanation: 학생 ends with a consonant, so the correct form is 이에요.

exercises.promptTranslation: Seoul is the capital of Korea ___
exercises.explanation: 수도 ends with a vowel, so the polite copula is 예요.

topics.title: Present Tense -아요/어요
topics.summary: Polite present tense adds -아요 to ㅏ/ㅗ stems, -어요 to other stems, and -해요 to 하다 verbs.
topics.explanation: To make the polite present tense, attach -아요 to verb stems whose last vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ, and -어요 to other stems. Verbs ending in 하다 become 해요. For example 가다 → 가요, 먹다 → 먹어요, 공부하다 → 공부해요.

examples.translation: I exercise every day.
My friend reads a book.
We drink water.

exercises.promptTranslation: I go to school.
exercises.explanation: 가다 has the vowel ㅏ, so it becomes 가요.

exercises.promptTranslation: My sibling eats.
exercises.explanation: 먹다 has no ㅏ/ㅗ, so it takes -어요 → 먹어요.

exercises.promptTranslation: We study Korean.
exercises.explanation: 하다 verbs become 해요, so 공부하다 → 공부해요.

exercises.promptTranslation: That person drinks coffee.
exercises.explanation: 마시다 + -어요 contracts to 마셔요.

topics.title: Past Tense -았/었어요
topics.summary: Polite past tense in Korean is formed with -았어요, -었어요, or -했어요.
topics.explanation: To make a verb polite past, add -았어요 after a vowel, -었어요 after a consonant, and -했어요 after 하다. The choice depends on the verb stem's final sound. This form is used in everyday conversation. Remember the vowel harmony: 아 afterㅏ orㅗ, 어 after other vowels.

examples.translation: I read a book yesterday.
She ate rice.
We watched a movie.

exercises.promptTranslation: I ___ at a cafe with a friend yesterday.
exercises.explanation: Use -았어요 after the vowel ㄱ to form the past polite.

exercises.promptTranslation: He ___ exercise every day.
exercises.explanation: For 하다, the past polite is -했어요.

exercises.promptTranslation: I ___ early in the morning.
exercises.explanation: The verb 일어나다 takes -았어요 because the stem ends with ㄴ (a consonant).

exercises.promptTranslation: She ___ the exam.
exercises.explanation: After the vowel ㅂ, use -았어요 for the past polite.

topics.title: Negation 안 and -지 않다
topics.summary: Negate a verb with 안 before it, or by attaching -지 않다 to the stem.
topics.explanation: There are two ways to negate. Put 안 directly before the verb (안 가요 = "don’t go"), or attach -지 않다 to the verb stem (가지 않아요). Both mean the same thing; 안 is more colloquial.

examples.translation: I don't go.
She doesn't eat.
My friend doesn't come.

exercises.promptTranslation: I don't go today.
exercises.explanation: 안 before the verb makes it negative: 안 가요.

exercises.promptTranslation: She doesn't eat meat.
exercises.explanation: 안 먹어요 means "doesn’t eat."

exercises.promptTranslation: My friend doesn't go to school.
exercises.explanation: The -지 않다 pattern: 가지 않아요.

exercises.promptTranslation: It doesn't rain.
exercises.explanation: 오지 않아요 means "it doesn’t rain."

topics.title: Existence 있다 / 없다
topics.summary: Use 있다 and 없어요 to say something exists or does not exist.
topics.explanation: 있다 means "to exist" or "to have" and is used with the polite ending 있어요. 없어요 is the negative form meaning "does not exist" or "does not have." Place the verb after the location or object you are talking about. The sentence ends with the verb, not a particle.

examples.translation: There is a book on the desk.
There is no milk in the refrigerator.
There is a cat in our house.

exercises.promptTranslation: There is a pen on the desk.
exercises.explanation: Use 있어요 to state that the pen exists.

exercises.promptTranslation: There is milk in the refrigerator.
exercises.explanation: 없어요 is the correct negative form because the sentence says there is no milk.

exercises.promptTranslation: There is a cat in our house.
exercises.explanation: 없어요 is used to say the cat does not exist in the house.

exercises.promptTranslation: There are trees in the park.
exercises.explanation: 있다 is the plain form used to state existence of trees.

topics.title: Location Particles 에 / 에서
topics.summary: Use 에 for a destination or static location, and 에서 for the place where an action happens.
topics.explanation: 에 marks a destination (가다/오다) or where something exists (있다/없다). 에서 marks the place where an action takes place. So you go 학교에 (to school) but study 학교에서 (at school).

examples.translation: I go to school.
I study at the library.
I am at home.

exercises.promptTranslation: I read a book at the library.
exercises.explanation: Reading is an action, so the place takes 에서.

exercises.promptTranslation: I go to school.
exercises.explanation: 가다 takes a destination, so 학교 takes 에.

exercises.promptTranslation: I exercise at the park.
exercises.explanation: Exercising is an action done at the park, so 에서.

exercises.promptTranslation: I am at home.
exercises.explanation: 있다 marks a static location with 에.

topics.title: Want to -고 싶다
topics.summary: Use -고 싶다 after a verb stem to say you want to do something.
topics.explanation: Take the verb stem and add 고 싶다 to express desire. In polite speech, change 싶다 to 싶어요. The construction works with any action verb. Use the appropriate verb stem before 고.

examples.translation: I want to read a book.
I want to watch a movie with my friend.
I want to study Korean tomorrow.

exercises.promptTranslation: I want coffee.
exercises.explanation: Use 마시고 싶어요 after 마시다 to express wanting to drink.

exercises.promptTranslation: She wants to travel.
exercises.explanation: 가고 싶어요 follows 가다 for wanting to travel.

exercises.promptTranslation: We want to wake up early tomorrow.
exercises.explanation: 고 싶어요 is the polite form after 일어나다.

exercises.promptTranslation: The children want to play in the park.
exercises.explanation: 놀고 싶어요 uses the verb 놀다 plus 고 싶어요.

topics.title: Connective -고 (and / then)
topics.summary: -고 connects two actions or clauses in sequence, meaning “and then”.
topics.explanation: Place -고 after the verb stem to link it with the next action. It shows that the second action happens after the first. The two clauses share the same subject unless otherwise marked. Use -고 in informal and formal speech alike.

examples.translation: I woke up in the morning and drank coffee.
I met a friend and watched a movie.
I finished the homework and went home.

exercises.promptTranslation: I eat ___ study.
exercises.explanation: -고 links the two actions, showing they happen sequentially.

exercises.promptTranslation: I read a book ___ listen to music.
exercises.explanation: -고 connects the verb ‘읽다’ with the following clause.

exercises.promptTranslation: I exercise ___ take a shower.
exercises.explanation: -고 is used to join the two actions in order.

exercises.promptTranslation: I opened the door ___ entered the room.
exercises.explanation: -고 links opening the door with entering the room.

topics.title: Honorifics -(으)시-
topics.summary: -(으)시- is added to verb stems to honorify the subject of the sentence.
topics.explanation: Attach -(으)시- directly after the verb stem when the subject is someone you respect. It works with all verb endings, including -아요/어요 and -습니다. The honorific does not change the meaning of the verb, only shows respect.

examples.translation: Grandmother drank the tea.
The teacher gave a presentation at the meeting.
Father returned home.

exercises.promptTranslation: Grandfather read the book.
exercises.explanation: -(으)시- is the honorific suffix to attach to 읽다.

exercises.promptTranslation: The professor explained in the lecture.
exercises.explanation: -(으)시- honors the verb 설명하다.

exercises.promptTranslation: The CEO entered the conference room.
exercises.explanation: -(으)시- is added to 들어오다 for respect.

exercises.promptTranslation: Mother prepared dinner.
exercises.explanation: -(으)시- honors the verb 준비하다.

topics.title: Can / Cannot -(으)ㄹ 수 있다/없다
topics.summary: -(으)ㄹ 수 있다/없다 says someone can or cannot do something — -을 수 after a consonant, -ㄹ 수 after a vowel.
topics.explanation: Attach -을 수 있다 to a verb stem ending in a consonant and -ㄹ 수 있다 to a stem ending in a vowel; swap 있다 for 없다 to say "cannot". Stems ending in ㄹ just add 수 (만들다 → 만들 수 있어요). It expresses both ability and possibility.

examples.translation: I can speak Korean.
You can't take photos here.
Can we meet tomorrow?

exercises.promptTranslation: I can eat kimchi.
exercises.explanation: 먹 ends in a consonant, so -을 수 있다 gives 먹을 수 있어요.

exercises.promptTranslation: I can't swim.
exercises.explanation: 하 ends in a vowel, so -ㄹ is attached: 할 수 없어요.

exercises.promptTranslation: I can make a cake.
exercises.explanation: 만들다 ends in ㄹ, so only 수 is added: 만들 수 있어요.

exercises.promptTranslation: I'm busy today, so I can't go.
exercises.explanation: 가 ends in a vowel, so -ㄹ is attached: 갈 수 없어요.

topics.title: Must -아/어야 하다
topics.summary: -아/어야 하다 means "have to / must" and follows the same vowel harmony as -아요/어요.
topics.explanation: Take the -아요/어요 form of a verb, drop 요, and add 야 하다 (or 야 되다 in speech): 가요 → 가야 해요, 먹어요 → 먹어야 해요, 공부해요 → 공부해야 해요. Tense goes on 하다, so 가야 했어요 means "had to go".

examples.translation: I have to get up early tomorrow.
I have to do my homework.
I had to go to the hospital yesterday.

exercises.promptTranslation: I have to take medicine.
exercises.explanation: 먹 has the vowel ㅓ, so -어야: 먹어야 해요.

exercises.promptTranslation: I have to go home now.
exercises.explanation: 가 + 아야 contracts to 가야.

exercises.promptTranslation: I have an exam, so I have to study.
exercises.explanation: 하다 verbs become 해야: 공부해야 해요.

exercises.promptTranslation: I have to read this book.
exercises.explanation: 읽 has the vowel ㅣ (not ㅏ/ㅗ), so -어야: 읽어야 해요.

topics.title: Because -아서/어서
topics.summary: -아서/어서 gives a reason or cause ("because / so") using the same vowel harmony as -아요/어요.
topics.explanation: Drop 요 from the -아요/어요 form and add 서: 바빠요 → 바빠서, 먹어요 → 먹어서, 피곤해요 → 피곤해서. Never put past tense before it (not 갔어서) — tense goes on the final verb only. It also cannot be followed by a command or suggestion; use -(으)니까 for those.

examples.translation: I was hungry, so I ate.
I was tired, so I went to bed early.
It rained, so I stayed home.

exercises.promptTranslation: The weather was nice, so I took a walk.
exercises.explanation: 좋 has the vowel ㅗ, so -아서: 좋아서. Past tense never goes before -아서.

exercises.promptTranslation: I had a headache, so I took medicine.
exercises.explanation: 아프다 drops ㅡ and becomes 아파서.

exercises.promptTranslation: I didn't have time, so I couldn't go.
exercises.explanation: 없 has the vowel ㅓ, so -어서: 없어서.

exercises.promptTranslation: I had a lot of work, so I was late.
exercises.explanation: 많 has the vowel ㅏ, so -아서: 많아서.

topics.title: If -(으)면
topics.summary: -(으)면 means "if / when" — -으면 after a consonant, -면 after a vowel or ㄹ.
topics.explanation: Attach -으면 to a stem ending in a consonant and -면 to a stem ending in a vowel or ㄹ: 먹다 → 먹으면, 가다 → 가면, 살다 → 살면. The -(으)면 clause states the condition and the second clause states the result.

examples.translation: If you have time, let's go together.
If it rains, use an umbrella.

examples.text: 한국에 살면 한국어를 빨리 배울 거예요.
examples.romanization: hanguge salmyeon hangugeoreul ppalli baeul geoyeyo.
examples.translation: If you live in Korea, you'll learn Korean quickly.

exercises.promptTranslation: If you take this medicine, you'll feel better.
exercises.explanation: 먹 ends in a consonant, so -으면: 먹으면.

exercises.promptTranslation: If you're tired, get some rest.
exercises.explanation: 하 ends in a vowel, so -면: 피곤하면.

exercises.promptTranslation: If you come to Seoul, get in touch.
exercises.explanation: 오 ends in a vowel, so -면: 오면.

exercises.promptTranslation: If you open the window, it's cool.
exercises.explanation: 열다 ends in ㄹ, so only -면 is added: 열면.

topics.title: Indirect Speech -다고 하다
topics.summary: Report what someone said with -다고 하다: -ㄴ/는다고 for action verbs, -다고 for adjectives, and -(이)라고 for nouns.
topics.explanation: Present-tense action verbs take -는다고 after a consonant stem and -ㄴ다고 after a vowel stem (먹는다고, 간다고). Adjectives and 있다/없다 take -다고 (바쁘다고, 있다고), the past uses -았/었다고 (갔다고), and nouns take -(이)라고 (학생이라고, 의사라고). In speech -다고 해요 often shortens to -대요.

examples.translation: My friend said they are coming tomorrow.
Minsu says they are busy.
That person said they are a student.

exercises.promptTranslation: My younger sibling said they are eating now.
exercises.explanation: 먹다 is an action verb with a consonant stem, so -는다고: 먹는다고.

exercises.promptTranslation: My friend said it is cold outside.
exercises.explanation: 춥다 is an adjective, so it takes -다고 directly: 춥다고.

exercises.promptTranslation: That person said they are a doctor.
exercises.explanation: 의사 is a noun ending in a vowel, so -라고: 의사라고.

exercises.promptTranslation: Mom said she went to the market yesterday.
exercises.explanation: A past event is reported with -았/었다고: 갔다고.

topics.title: Recalling Experience -더라고요
topics.summary: -더라고요 shares something you saw, heard or felt first-hand in the past — like "I noticed that…".
topics.explanation: Attach -더라고요 directly to a verb or adjective stem (맛있더라고요, 많더라고요) and -(이)더라고요 to nouns. It reports something you discovered through your own experience, so the subject is usually someone or something other than yourself. It sounds conversational and invites the listener into your experience.

examples.translation: The food at that restaurant was really good (I found).
Seoul had so many people (I noticed).
Minji sings well (I heard it myself).

exercises.promptTranslation: That movie was really fun (I found).
exercises.explanation: -더라고요 shares a first-hand experience: 재미있더라고요.

exercises.promptTranslation: It was really windy on Jeju (I noticed).
exercises.explanation: 불다 + -더라고요 → 불더라고요, reporting what you experienced.

exercises.promptTranslation: Korean people eat spicy food well (I noticed).
exercises.explanation: You are sharing an observation, so 먹더라고요.

exercises.promptTranslation: That shop was closed on Sunday (I saw).
exercises.explanation: 닫다 + -더라고요 → 닫더라고요, something you saw yourself.

topics.title: Expectation -(으)ㄹ 텐데
topics.summary: -(으)ㄹ 텐데 expresses an expectation that sets up what you say next — "it must/would be…, so…".
topics.explanation: Attach -을 텐데 after a consonant stem and -ㄹ 텐데 after a vowel stem (먹을 텐데, 바쁠 텐데); nouns take 일 텐데. The speaker assumes something is likely and uses it as background for advice, worry or a wish. Ending a sentence with -(으)ㄹ 텐데요 leaves a hopeful or worried tone.

examples.translation: You'll probably be busy tomorrow, so get to bed early.
You must be hungry — have this.
It would be nice if I had time.

exercises.prompt: 그 사람은 지금 ___ 텐데 나중에 전화하세요.
exercises.promptTranslation: They're probably working now, so call later.
exercises.explanation: 하 ends in a vowel, so -ㄹ 텐데: 일할 텐데.

exercises.promptTranslation: It's probably cold outside, so wear a coat.
exercises.explanation: 춥다 is ㅂ-irregular: 춥 + 을 → 추울 텐데.

exercises.promptTranslation: You must be very tired, so rest a little.
exercises.explanation: 하 ends in a vowel, so -ㄹ 텐데: 피곤할 텐데.

exercises.promptTranslation: The food is probably hot, so eat slowly.
exercises.explanation: 뜨겁다 is ㅂ-irregular: 뜨겁 + 을 → 뜨거울 텐데.

topics.title: Passive Verbs -이/히/리/기-
topics.summary: Passive verbs add -이-, -히-, -리- or -기- to certain stems, turning "do" into "be done".
topics.explanation: Which suffix a verb takes has to be learned: 보다 → 보이다 (be seen), 닫다 → 닫히다 (be closed), 듣다 → 들리다 (be heard), 열다 → 열리다 (be opened), 안다 → 안기다 (be held). The thing affected becomes the subject with 이/가, and the doer, if mentioned, takes 에게 or 한테. Most 하다 verbs use 되다 instead (사용하다 → 사용되다).

examples.translation: The door opened.
You can see the mountain well from here.
The child was held by its mother.

exercises.promptTranslation: The writing on the board is easy to see.
exercises.explanation: 보다 takes -이- in the passive: 보이다 → 보여요.

exercises.promptTranslation: The window closed because of the wind.
exercises.explanation: 닫다 takes -히- in the passive: 닫히다 → 닫혔어요.

exercises.promptTranslation: I can't hear the phone well.
exercises.explanation: 듣다 takes -리- in the passive: 들리다 → 들려요.

exercises.promptTranslation: The baby was held in its mother's arms.
exercises.explanation: 안다 takes -기- in the passive: 안기다 → 안겼어요.
